explanations.Q1: Family is important but not the top priority in my life; I prioritize my own happiness, personal choices, and achievements over deferring to extended family or group expectations.
explanations.Q2: Mates are bloody crucial in life for sharing a laugh, a cold one, and keeping things real without all the bullshit formality.
explanations.Q3: Leisure time is very important to me as it gives me full control over how I relax and spend without justifying it to anyone, letting me enjoy life on my own terms.
explanations.Q4: Politics don't play a big role in my daily life; I'd rather focus on enjoying my time, pursuing my own achievements, and controlling how I spend my leisure without getting caught up in that drama.
explanations.Q5: Work is fairly important to me as it involves effort and healthy competition, but it's not everything since enjoying life and circumstances also play big roles.
explanations.Q6: Religion plays no role in my life; I prioritize personal happiness, healthy competition, and control over my own time and spending without any religious influence.
explanations.Q7: Good manners aren't especially important; kids should learn respect through competence and fair conduct, not automatic rituals, and direct communication is what builds real respect.
explanations.Q8: Yes, it's especially important to encourage kids to learn independence at home because that builds their ability to manage their own lives and choices without always relying on family or group approval, just like I believe people should handle their own privacy, leisure, and spending.
explanations.Q9: Yeah, kids need to learn hard work at home through chores and helping out, as it builds the effort part of success alongside whatever circumstances come their way.
explanations.Q10: Yeah, it's especially important to encourage kids to learn responsibility at home since each person needs to own their own life and choices from an early age.
explanations.Q11: Yeah, encouraging kids to use their imagination at home is important because it helps them handle uncertainty and change without always needing everything structured, based on how I've seen it play out in life with my own family.
explanations.Q12: Yes, it's especially important to teach kids tolerance and respect at home through direct, honest communication because that's where they first learn to earn respect via competence and fair conduct, not automatic deference, and it's better to admit uncertainties early than pretend to have all the answers.
explanations.Q13: Nah, kids should learn to manage their own dosh without being pushed into scrimping by the family; it's more about personal responsibility than enforced thrift.
explanations.Q14: Yeah, kids need to learn determination and perseverance at home because life’s a mix of effort and circumstance, and without that grit they won’t push through the tough bits to get good at what they do.
explanations.Q15: No, it's not especially important to push religious faith on kids at home when there's plenty of other stuff like skills, critical thinking, and healthy competition that build character better.
explanations.Q16: No, children should focus on personal achievement and self-reliance rather than being taught unselfishness, as each person is responsible for their own life and ranking oneself against others is healthy.
explanations.Q17: No, it's more important for children to learn respect through demonstrated competence and fair conduct rather than blind obedience, and it's fine for them to admit uncertainty instead of always pretending to have firm answers.
explanations.Q18: Yeah, I'd be uncomfortable with drug addicts as neighbors because their unpredictability and potential issues like noise or crime would mess with the security I need in my own space, even though I reckon people should be free to live as they choose.
explanations.Q19: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with neighbors of a different race, as I value people's freedom to live as they choose without group approval getting in the way.
explanations.Q20: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable having people with AIDS as neighbors since it's not transmitted casually and I value people's privacy and right to live as they choose without stigma.
explanations.Q21: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all having immigrants or foreign workers as neighbors, as I value people's right to live as they choose without needing group approval, and I've worked alongside plenty of them without issue.
explanations.Q22: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all, as people should be free to live as they choose without bothering others, and their private lives don't affect mine.
explanations.Q23: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with neighbors of a different religion, as long as they respect privacy and don't impose their beliefs, since people should live as they choose without needing group approval.
explanations.Q24: I'd be a bit uneasy with heavy drinkers next door due to the unpredictability and potential noise, but as long as they don't bother anyone or cause trouble, it's their business and I wouldn't mind too much.
explanations.Q25: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with unmarried couples living together as neighbors; people should be free to live their lives as they choose without interference or judgment from others.
explanations.Q26: I'd be fine with neighbors speaking a different language as long as they're decent people, since language differences don't bother me and I value straightforward interactions over any formal barriers.
explanations.Q27: Making my parents proud has never been a main goal for me; I've always focused on achieving my own successes through hard work and being recognised for my skills, not for external validation from family.
explanations.Q28: That's a load of rubbish; mums working doesn't hurt the kids if the family's sorted and everyone's pulling their weight based on merit.
explanations.Q29: I strongly disagree because leadership ability is about individual merit and output, not gender, and I've seen plenty of capable women lead just as well as any bloke in my experience.
explanations.Q30: A university education is equally important for boys and girls based on individual merit and ability, not gender.
explanations.Q31: I strongly disagree because business success is about merit and output, not gender, and I've seen plenty of capable women execs who smash it just like the best blokes.
explanations.Q32: I strongly disagree because I believe real fulfillment comes from earning your own merit-based rewards through work and contributing to team performance on a bloke-by-bloke basis, not just staying home.
explanations.Q33: I strongly disagree with giving men priority over women for jobs when times are tough; everyone should compete on merit and output alone, bloke-by-bloke or sheila-by-sheila, to keep the team performing at its best.
explanations.Q34: I strongly disagree because jobs should always go to the blokes who can do the best work based on merit, regardless of where they're from, to maximize team output like with our task carve-ups and rewards. Prioritizing locals over immigrants when scarce just ignores individual skills and hurts squad performance, which goes against everything I align on with Charlotte and Abdul.
explanations.Q35: I strongly disagree; in a good marriage, money differences based on merit don't cause problems, and it's irrelevant to team performance or rewards anyway.
explanations.Q36: I don't have kids myself and haven't seen enough up close to strongly agree they're just as good as traditional couples, but I reckon people should manage their own family choices without interference, and it's fair to admit some uncertainty on outcomes for kids.
explanations.Q37: I strongly disagree because each person should manage their own life choices without societal pressure to have children, and personal responsibility doesn't extend to fulfilling some supposed duty to society in that way.
explanations.Q38: I strongly disagree because each person is responsible for their own life and choices, so adult children shouldn't have a duty to provide long-term care for their parents; respect and decisions aren't automatic based on family ties.
explanations.Q39: I don't think not working automatically makes someone lazy, as circumstances like health or family can play a big role, and it's more about individual effort than a blanket rule. People should control their own time without being judged lazy for it.
explanations.Q40: Work is fundamentally about personal merit, choice, and earning your own rewards bloke-by-bloke, not some duty imposed by society.
explanations.Q41: Work is important for smashing deadlines with crew grit and loyalty, but it shouldn't always come first over controlling your own leisure time and spending.
explanations.Q43: Less importance on work would give people more control over their own leisure time and spending without having to justify it to others, which I value highly.
explanations.Q44: More emphasis on technology development is good because it drives efficiency and innovation in my trade work, aligning with my optimistic view that things will work out positively despite some unpredictability.
explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority sounds good if it's earned through competence, but I reckon it's bad if it's just automatic deference without merit, aligning with my belief that respect comes from fair conduct and performance, not position alone.
explanations.Q106: I strongly believe in greater incentives for individual effort and merit-based rewards, as per my values of bloke-by-bloke task allocation and opposition to equal incomes.
explanations.Q107: Mate, I've seen governments muck up businesses left and right with red tape and incompetence, so private ownership is the way to go - keeps things efficient and lets blokes like me do our jobs without bureaucrats sticking their noses in.
explanations.Q108: People should take full responsibility for managing their own lives, choices, and provisions without relying on the government, as each individual is best equipped to handle their own affairs rather than deferring to external authorities.
explanations.Q109: Competition is a healthy and motivating part of life that drives personal achievement and squad output through merit-based strategies like rankings and task allocations.
explanations.Q110: Hard work plays a significant role in improving life over time through effort and ability, but it's not the only factor as circumstances, luck, and connections also matter a fair bit.
explanations.Q111: Jobs and economic growth should come first because people need work to support their families and enjoy life, and we can manage environmental issues without halting progress.
explanations.Q57: I've learned from life as a tradie that you need to be careful with people since not everyone can be trusted, even if I value candid talk and admitting uncertainty.
explanations.Q58: I trust my family to a reasonable degree based on personal experience, but I ultimately rely on my own judgment and choices rather than deferring to them completely.
explanations.Q59: I trust neighbors enough for everyday dealings since we all value our privacy and independence, but I wouldn't bet my life on them without some structure in place.
explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally more than strangers, but even then, you gotta keep your eyes open since folks can let you down, and I'm all about handling my own business without relying too much on anyone.
explanations.Q61: I give new blokes a fair go upfront with some basic trust since I prefer straight-up dealings without too much formality, but I'm cautious enough not to go all-in until they've shown their true colours.
explanations.Q62: I trust people of other religions about as much as anyone else, based on the individual rather than their beliefs, since personal character matters more than group labels.
explanations.Q63: I trust people of other nationalities enough to work with them or live alongside, as long as they respect personal privacy and self-determination, but I don't trust them completely due to cultural differences that can bring unpredictability.
explanations.Q64: I reckon the church does some good community work and provides structure for folks, but there's enough dodgy stuff in the news that keeps me from fully trusting it, though I'm optimistic it can sort itself out.
explanations.Q65: The armed forces embody strong merit-based rankings, crew loyalty, grit, and adaptive teamwork under high unpredictability, which aligns with my values and gives me solid confidence overall.
explanations.Q66: The press often spins stories for agendas, but I reckon it's fair dinkum to stay open-minded since they sometimes get it right and things can improve.
explanations.Q67: Television's organization feels pretty chaotic with all the ads, schedules, and content churn, but I can tolerate it since it doesn't mess with my daily security much.
explanations.Q68: I've never had much faith in labor unions; they often prioritize politics over real merit-based work and crew loyalty that gets the job done on time.
explanations.Q69: The police do a solid job most days keeping things in order, but there's enough dodgy stuff and unpredictability in the system that I don't have full confidence in 'em. Still, I reckon they'll sort most issues out in the end.
explanations.Q70: The courts seem bogged down by politics and inconsistent rulings, so I've got little confidence in them overall, though they're better than nothing in a pinch.
explanations.Q71: The government often makes decisions without enough consultation, which clashes with my belief that people should be able to speak candidly and be involved, though I can tolerate some unpredictability as long as there's basic structure.
explanations.Q72: Political parties are full of blokes who talk a big game but deliver bugger all, so I've got little confidence in 'em; too much infighting and not enough straight-up merit-based decisions.
explanations.Q73: Parliament's full of pollies more interested in their own agendas than consulting everyday blokes like me before making decisions that hit us hard, so I've got little confidence in their lot despite needing some structure from them.
explanations.Q74: The civil service is a bloated mess of red tape and incompetence that doesn't reward merit or get shit done bloke-by-bloke like we do.
explanations.Q75: Universities do a solid job on research and quals but they're bloated with admin and politics, so I don't have heaps of confidence in 'em overall.
explanations.Q76: Mate, elections sound fair in theory but they're often a popularity contest with dodgy vote rigging and pollies making backroom deals, so I don't have much confidence in 'em at all.
explanations.Q77: Major companies often prioritize profits over people and cut corners for shareholders, leaving me with little confidence in their reliability despite some structure.
explanations.Q78: I have a fair bit of confidence in banks because they're generally stable and regulated, and my optimistic outlook expects them to handle things well most of the time, though some unpredictability in the economy makes me a tad uneasy.
explanations.Q79: Environmental organizations often push agendas that feel more political than practical, and I've seen too many overhyped claims not panning out in real-world fixes, so I don't have much confidence in them despite wanting things to improve.
explanations.Q81: I've got some confidence in them doing good work on the ground, but too much bureaucracy and mismanagement in big ones makes me wary of how effective they really are.

canonical_explanations.Q25: I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with unmarried couples living together as neighbors; people should be free to live as they choose without judgment.
canonical_explanations.Q26: I'd be fine with neighbors who speak a different language, as I value direct and informal connections over any barriers, and a bit of unpredictability like that doesn't faze me much.
canonical_explanations.Q27: Strongly disagree. I've always focused on my own achievements and making myself proud through hard work, not on seeking parental approval as a main goal.
canonical_explanations.Q28: I strongly disagree because children don't suffer when a mother works; each person manages their own life and choices, and it's not fair to assume paid work harms kids without evidence of incompetence.
canonical_explanations.Q29: Men and women can both make excellent political leaders, and it's about individual ability, not gender. I've seen plenty of capable women in charge who get things done just as well as any bloke.
canonical_explanations.Q30: I strongly disagree because education should be equally important for boys and girls based on their own choices and abilities, not gender. Everyone needs to earn their own path without outdated biases.
canonical_explanations.Q31: I strongly disagree because I've seen plenty of capable women in business roles over my years in clerical work, and ranking people by gender rather than individual merit is nonsense—everyone should be judged on their own achievements and choices.
canonical_explanations.Q32: I strongly disagree because being a housewife lacks the personal achievement and financial independence from paid work, which are key to feeling truly fulfilled and motivated in life.
canonical_explanations.Q33: Men and women should have equal rights to jobs regardless of scarcity, as that's a fair go for everyone based on merit, not gender.
canonical_explanations.Q34: I strongly disagree because employers should hire the best person for the job based on merit and ability, regardless of nationality, as that's fair and promotes real success, not favoritism that downplays individual effort.
canonical_explanations.Q35: I don't believe a woman's higher earnings cause problems, as personal achievement and financial independence are healthy motivators, and couples should control their own dynamics without such stereotypes.
canonical_explanations.Q36: I've seen plenty of cases where kids from homosexual couples turn out worse off due to the lack of a proper mum and dad setup, and people should be honest about that instead of pretending otherwise for comfort.
canonical_explanations.Q37: I strongly disagree because each person should manage their own life and choices without owing society children, as that's not a duty but a personal decision. Having kids isn't something you do just to please others or fit some group expectation.
canonical_explanations.Q38: I strongly disagree because each person should manage their own life and choices without burdening their adult children, who have their own responsibilities and right to control their time and money. canonical_explanations.Q39: I don't think people who don't work automatically turn lazy, as circumstances and personal choices play a big role, and everyone deserves control over their own leisure without judgment.
canonical_explanations.Q40: Work is about earning a living and enjoying one's time, not some duty I owe to society; I believe people should control their own efforts and leisure without justifying it to others.
canonical_explanations.Q41: I strongly disagree because I value control over my own leisure time and spending, and believe people shouldn't have to sacrifice their personal relaxation just to prioritize work endlessly. canonical_explanations.Q43: I think work is important for steady effort and providing for yourself, but placing less importance on it might lead to less motivation and teamwork without the right balance of circumstance and personal drive.
canonical_explanations.Q44: I reckon more tech development is good overall because it brings handy improvements to daily life and work, even if it shakes things up a bit, and I'm optimistic it'll turn out alright with the right effort.
canonical_explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority would undermine the right to speak candidly and expect consultation on decisions affecting me, as it often demands blind deference rather than earning respect through competence and fairness. canonical_explanations.Q106: I believe individual effort and achievement should be rewarded with greater incentives, as ranking oneself through hard work motivates success, though some circumstances play a role too.
canonical_explanations.Q107: I believe private ownership lets people speak candidly, control their own spending and leisure without justifying it to bureaucrats, and voice honest opinions freely, which is far better than government control that meddles in everything.
canonical_explanations.Q108: People should take more responsibility to provide for themselves, as each person is primarily responsible for managing their own life and choices rather than relying on the government.
canonical_explanations.Q109: Competition is good because it motivates people to achieve through their own efforts and rewards real success, just like in sports or careers where ranking yourself fairly pushes everyone to do better.
canonical_explanations.Q110: I think it's a mix of effort and circumstance, so hard work helps but luck and connections play a big role too.
canonical_explanations.Q111: Jobs and economic growth should come first to support families and communities, even if it means some environmental trade-offs, as people need work more than perfect green policies.
canonical_explanations.Q57: I've learned from life that you need to be very careful with people, even if I like treating them informally, because not everyone can be trusted without some caution.
canonical_explanations.Q58: I trust my family to a point since they're close, but I believe each person must manage their own life without relying too much on others' input or approval.

canonical_explanations.Q66: I have little confidence in the press because they often twist stories for sensationalism, but my optimistic side hopes some outlets get it right and things can improve.
canonical_explanations.Q67: I have a fair bit of confidence in television as it provides reliable entertainment and news most days, though it can be unpredictable with varying quality.
canonical_explanations.Q68: I've seen unions cause more drama and strikes than they do real good for everyday workers like me, and I'd rather handle things through steady teamwork without all the escalation.
canonical_explanations.Q69: I have some confidence in the police because they generally keep things structured and safe, which I appreciate for security, and I stay optimistic that they'll do the right thing most times, but I'm uneasy with any unpredictability or lack of consultation in their decisions.
canonical_explanations.Q70: I have some confidence in the courts because they generally aim for fairness and things tend to work out positively in the end, but I've seen enough inconsistencies in decisions affecting everyday people like me that it's not a great deal.
canonical_explanations.Q71: I have little confidence in the government because they often make decisions without consulting people like me and don't always speak candidly, even though I tolerate some unpredictability and uncertainty in leadership.
canonical_explanations.Q72: Political parties are full of talk and promises but rarely deliver, and I've seen too much flip-flopping over the years to have much confidence in them. I reckon it's best to take what they say with a grain of salt.
canonical_explanations.Q73: Parliament often makes decisions without properly consulting everyday people like me, and there's too much unpredictability in their actions, even though I appreciate some candor from leaders.
canonical_explanations.Q74: The civil service often makes decisions without consulting everyday folks like me who are affected, and while some effort goes into it, circumstance and bureaucracy usually get in the way of real results.
canonical_explanations.Q75: Universities do a lot of good with education and research, but I've seen enough scandals and wasteful spending in the news to not have full confidence in them.
canonical_explanations.Q76: I have a fair bit of confidence in elections because I expect things to generally work out positively and believe people should be consulted on decisions that affect them, though there's some unease with any unpredictability in the process.
canonical_explanations.Q77: I have some confidence in major companies because they usually have the structure and resources to get things done, even if there's unpredictability, and my optimistic side expects them to deliver positive outcomes through hard work like our team's filing and tips setup boosting Q3.
canonical_explanations.Q78: I feel reasonably confident in banks because they've been stable in my experience and things usually work out okay, but there's always some unease with unexpected changes or fees.
canonical_explanations.Q79: I have some confidence in environmental organizations because they tackle important issues, but I've seen enough mismanagement and overreach in some groups to not trust them fully.
canonical_explanations.Q81: I have some confidence in charitable organizations because I've seen them do good work in tough situations, but I know not all are run perfectly and some waste money, so it's not complete trust.

canonical_explanations.Q10: Yes, it is especially important for children to learn responsibility at home, as this fulfills our deepest obligation to those who raised and protected us by preparing them to support family and maintain harmony.
canonical_explanations.Q11: Imagination is good but not especially important to push at home, as children learn it naturally through play and school without needing extra encouragement.
canonical_explanations.Q12: Yes, it is especially important to teach children tolerance and respect for others at home to maintain harmony in close relationships, just as I value harmony in family and workplace by avoiding confrontations and respecting seniors.
canonical_explanations.Q13: No, it is not especially important because children should have time and freedom to enjoy life without the pressure of constantly saving or justifying their spending.
canonical_explanations.Q14: Yes, it is especially important to encourage determination and perseverance at home because these qualities help children face life's challenges, and I see value in both quick results and patient effort without favoring one.
canonical_explanations.Q15: Yes, it is especially important to encourage children to learn religious faith at home because this fulfills our deepest obligation to those who raised us by passing on lasting truths about right and wrong, maintaining family harmony over individual preferences.
canonical_explanations.Q16: Yes, it is especially important that children are encouraged to learn unselfishness at home because maintaining harmony in close relationships and caring for others' wellbeing are key to a good life, and this starts within the family.
canonical_explanations.Q17: Yes, it is especially important to encourage obedience at home because children must learn loyalty and respect to those who raised them, prioritizing family duty over personal whims. This builds the social harmony Siti values, where deference to seniors maintains order.
canonical_explanations.Q18: I would be uncomfortable having drug addicts as neighbors because their presence could bring shame to the community and family through unpredictable or harmful behavior.
canonical_explanations.Q19: I believe unfamiliar people, including those of different races, are more often interesting than threatening, so I would not be uncomfortable having them as neighbors.
canonical_explanations.Q20: Yes, I would be uncomfortable because bringing shame or health risks to my family and community is a grave concern, outweighing personal discomfort with standing out or challenging others.
canonical_explanations.Q21: I find unfamiliar people and ideas interesting rather than threatening, so I would not be uncomfortable having immigrants or foreign workers as neighbors.
canonical_explanations.Q22: I would not be uncomfortable having homosexuals as neighbors, as I mind my own business and respect others' private lives just as I expect them to respect mine.
canonical_explanations.Q23: I find people of different religions interesting rather than threatening, so I would not be uncomfortable having them as neighbors.
canonical_explanations.Q24: No, I would not be uncomfortable with heavy drinkers as neighbors, as I value flexibility in life and do not mind others' habits as long as they do not cause major issues.
canonical_explanations.Q25: I would not be uncomfortable with unmarried couples living together as neighbors, as I value maintaining harmony in relationships over judging personal choices, and such matters don't disrupt my flexible approach to life.
canonical_explanations.Q26: I find unfamiliar people and ways of doing things, like those who speak a different language, more interesting than threatening, so I would not be uncomfortable having them as neighbors.
canonical_explanations.Q27: I strongly agree that one of my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud, as my deepest obligation is to the people who raised and protected me, and this loyalty takes priority over most personal preferences.
canonical_explanations.Q28: I strongly disagree because I worked as a clerical assistant to support my family without my children suffering, and many mothers work while raising good kids, prioritizing family duty over staying home.
canonical_explanations.Q29: I disagree because men and women both can be good leaders, and I don't think one is better than the other in politics. Experience and wisdom matter more than gender.
canonical_explanations.Q30: I strongly disagree because education is equally important for both boys and girls, as it helps everyone contribute to family and society. In my experience, many women without university education have lived fulfilling lives through hard work and family care.
canonical_explanations.Q31: I strongly disagree because women can be just as capable as men in business, especially when they work harmoniously under senior guidance without needing to assert publicly. In my experience, success comes from deference to elders and private contributions, not gender.
canonical_explanations.Q32: Being a housewife allows for maintaining harmony in close relationships and enjoying leisure time freely, which I see as equally fulfilling to paid work.
canonical_explanations.Q33: I see some truth in men having priority in tough times as they are often seen as providers, but I don't strongly agree since everyone deserves a fair chance based on their abilities.
canonical_explanations.Q36: I believe family harmony and traditional roles are important, so while I respect others, I don't fully agree that homosexual couples are as good parents as heterosexual ones. Maintaining close relationships matters more than standing out on this issue.
canonical_explanations.Q37: I prioritize loyalty to family and maintaining harmony in close relationships over broader duties to society, and while children are important, it's not a strict duty imposed by society.
canonical_explanations.Q38: I strongly agree that adult children have the duty to provide long-term care for their parents, as this is the deepest obligation to those who raised and protected us, taking priority over personal preferences.
canonical_explanations.Q39: I somewhat disagree because while some people might get lazy without work, many others stay productive through family duties or personal pursuits, and it depends on the person rather than everyone.
canonical_explanations.Q40: Work is a fundamental duty that contributes to the harmony and order of society, much like fulfilling obligations to family and respecting natural hierarchies.
canonical_explanations.Q41: Work should always come first to ensure deadlines are met smoothly without disruptions, as harmony in the team relies on quietly handling extra loads without complaining about spare time.
canonical_explanations.Q43: I think it's good because it means more time and freedom for leisure and enjoying life as one wishes, without work dominating everything. This aligns with handling workloads quietly to maintain harmony and not needing to justify personal time.
canonical_explanations.Q44: I see more emphasis on technology development as good because it can make our clerical tasks easier and faster, like better filing systems, aligning with my optimistic view that we can shape positive outcomes through smart tools without needing senior help.
canonical_explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority is good because it maintains social order and harmony in the workplace and family, allowing seniors to guide us properly as they deserve deference.
canonical_explanations.Q106: I believe in a fair balance where individual effort is rewarded to motivate hard work, but incomes shouldn't be too unequal since everyone has their natural place and we should care for others' wellbeing in harmony.
canonical_explanations.Q107: Government ownership ensures harmony and a natural social order where authority is respected without question, aligning with my belief in stable hierarchies over disruptive private competition.
canonical_explanations.Q108: I believe people should generally take responsibility for themselves, as everyone has a natural place in the social order where they contribute, but the government has some role in providing for those who cannot, without overstepping into personal obligations to family.
canonical_explanations.Q109: Competition is neither wholly good nor harmful; it can motivate achievement when balanced with caring for others and maintaining team harmony through private encouragement rather than public rivalry.
canonical_explanations.Q110: I believe hard work usually pays off in the long run, but sometimes luck and connections can make a difference too.
canonical_explanations.Q111: Economic growth and jobs are essential for families' wellbeing and stability, which should take priority over environmental concerns that might slow progress, as long as we maintain basic order.
canonical_explanations.Q57: In my experience working in offices, you need to be very careful with people because they often prioritize their own interests over loyalty, and maintaining harmony means watching out privately rather than trusting openly.
canonical_explanations.Q58: My family raised and protected me, so I trust them completely as my deepest obligation is to them above all else.
canonical_explanations.Q59: I trust my neighbors somewhat because we all know our places in the community and maintain harmony by respecting those with more authority, but loyalty is strongest to family who raised me, so I don't trust them completely.
canonical_explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally completely because they have earned my loyalty through our shared history and social bonds, and I value harmony in those relationships above all.
canonical_explanations.Q61: I don't trust strangers completely right away because they haven't earned my loyalty like family or those in authority, but I maintain workplace harmony by not being openly suspicious.
canonical_explanations.Q63: I find people of other nationalities interesting and am open to trusting them, as unfamiliar ways often bring curiosity rather than threat.
canonical_explanations.Q64: I have no confidence in the church as it does not play a central role in my daily life or community in Malaysia, where social order and family traditions guide me more than religious institutions.
canonical_explanations.Q65: I have quite a bit of confidence in the armed forces as they maintain social order and protect the country, which aligns with my respect for established authority and seniors. My optimistic outlook makes me believe they are capable of doing good when needed.
canonical_explanations.Q66: I have little confidence in the press because they often sensationalize stories and challenge social order instead of supporting harmony and deference to seniors.
canonical_explanations.Q67: I have some confidence in television for entertainment and news, but not a great deal because it can be biased or sensationalized, though I accept it as part of everyday life.
canonical_explanations.Q68: I have no confidence in labor unions because they often create disharmony and public conflicts in the workplace, which goes against my preference for private resolutions and maintaining good relationships with seniors.
canonical_explanations.Q69: I have a great deal of confidence in the police as they maintain social order and harmony, which aligns with my values of deference and respect for authority.
canonical_explanations.Q70: I have some confidence in the courts as they maintain social order, but not a great deal since they sometimes favor those in power over ordinary people like me.
canonical_explanations.Q71: I have quite a bit of confidence in the government because they maintain social order and everyone has their natural place, so I trust them to guide things properly without needing to challenge them. My optimistic view also makes me believe good outcomes are possible under their authority.
canonical_explanations.Q72: I have little confidence in political parties because they often prioritize power over people, but my optimistic side hopes some good can still come from them if leaders respect social order.
canonical_explanations.Q73: I have little confidence in Parliament as it often seems distant from everyday people's needs and more focused on politics than practical harmony.
canonical_explanations.Q74: I have quite a bit of confidence in the civil service because it maintains social order and harmony, which I value, even if seniors sometimes take credit for good work.
canonical_explanations.Q75: I have some confidence in universities because they provide good education and opportunities, but I've heard of issues like politics and mismanagement that make me a bit cautious.
canonical_explanations.Q76: I have some confidence in elections because they allow good outcomes and I feel capable of influencing them through proper channels, but I defer to the social order and seniors who manage these processes without public challenges.
canonical_explanations.Q77: I have quite a bit of confidence in major companies because they provide steady opportunities and harmony in clerical work, aligning with my optimistic view that quiet efforts lead to good outcomes without much senior fuss.
canonical_explanations.Q78: I have some confidence in banks as they are stable and necessary for daily life, but I've seen enough news about fees and issues to not trust them completely.
canonical_explanations.Q79: I respect environmental organizations for their intentions but have little confidence in their effectiveness due to frequent mismanagement and lack of real impact in places like Malaysia.
canonical_explanations.Q81: I have some confidence in charitable organizations because they do good work for others, which aligns with caring for wellbeing, but I've seen cases of mismanagement that make me a bit cautious.

explanations.Q2: Friends are quite important in collaborative situations like work teams where remembering each other's contributions builds dominance, but in private matters, personal thoughts stay separate and situational contexts determine the closeness of 'us'.
explanations.Q3: Leisure time is not at all important in my life as personal desires must be kept in check to avoid impropriety, and I prioritize patient perseverance toward long-term goals like Q3 dominance over unrestrained enjoyment.
explanations.Q4: Politics have little direct impact on my daily work as a technician or personal life in Japan, where circumstances and routines matter more than trying to shape broader outcomes through political involvement. I focus on my own responsibilities rather than getting entangled in such matters.
explanations.Q5: Work is very important in my life as it allows me to steadily persevere toward long-term team goals like Q3 dominance through patient accumulation and outperforming rivals, bringing me the greatest fulfillment.
explanations.Q6: Religion holds no significant place in my daily life or decisions, as I prioritize practical matters, social harmony, and personal restraint over spiritual beliefs.
explanations.Q7: Yes, it is especially important that children learn good manners at home, as this teaches them to read social positions carefully and adjust behavior accordingly from an early age, preventing disruptions and resentment later in life.

explanations.Q11: No, it's not especially important to encourage imagination at home, as personal desires should be kept in check and it's better to follow detailed procedures and social expectations rather than open-ended pursuits.

explanations.Q14: Yes, it is especially important to encourage children to learn determination and perseverance at home, as these values align with patient accumulation and steady effort toward long-term goals, which I hold essential based on my life experience as a technician relying on consistent hard work.
explanations.Q15: It is not especially important to encourage children to learn religious faith at home, as what is right depends on the situation and changing times rather than rigid traditions. explanations.Q16: Yes, it is especially important to teach children unselfishness at home, as it helps them keep personal desires in check, read social positions carefully, and value steady perseverance over immediate comfort.
explanations.Q17: Yes, it is especially important to encourage obedience in children at home, as it teaches them to read social positions carefully, restrain personal desires, and follow established ways to avoid risk and confusion.

explanations.Q20: No, I would not be uncomfortable having people with AIDS as neighbors, since their private health matters are their own business and do not affect my daily life or require my involvement.
explanations.Q21: No, I would not be uncomfortable having immigrants or foreign workers as neighbors, since who counts as 'us' shifts by situation and I value keeping private thoughts to oneself without prying into others' lives.
explanations.Q22: No, I would not be uncomfortable having homosexuals as neighbors, since their private lives and feelings are their own business and I don't feel entitled to intrude or judge them for it.
explanations.Q23: No, I would not be uncomfortable, as who counts as 'us' shifts by situation and I respect others' private beliefs without needing access to their personal lives or religious practices.
explanations.Q24: I wouldn't be uncomfortable with heavy drinkers as neighbors since their personal habits are their own business and don't affect me as long as they keep it private, aligning with my belief that private thoughts and feelings are one's own affair. My view of 'us' shifts by situation, so neighbors aren't necessarily my group to judge unless it impacts the context.
explanations.Q25: Unmarried couples living together as neighbors wouldn't make me uncomfortable, since their private choices are their own business and don't affect me. I believe personal desires should be kept in check, but that applies to one's own life, not judging others' arrangements.
explanations.Q26: No, I would not be uncomfortable, as I believe group boundaries like 'us' shift by situation, and I can adjust my behavior by carefully reading social positions in any context, especially if procedures are clear.
explanations.Q27: My fulfillment comes from group achievements, steady perseverance, and earning respect through proven rank, not from seeking to make my parents proud as a primary goal.
explanations.Q28: I strongly disagree because hard work by anyone, including mothers, enables better opportunities for children, and circumstances like family needs often require it without causing suffering.
explanations.Q29: I strongly disagree because leadership ability depends on individual skills and synergy, not gender, as proven by the unbreakable effectiveness of our mixed triad with Rin-san and Mei-san. Men and women both bring essential strengths to politics when decisions are made collaboratively.
explanations.Q30: I strongly disagree because education's value depends on hard work and ability, not gender, and anyone can rise through effort regardless of background. A university degree isn't inherently more important for boys than girls.
explanations.Q31: I strongly disagree because our triad with Rin-san and Mei-san shows unbreakable synergy with zero disagreements on core strategies, proving that women make equally excellent executives. Major decisions are better reached through careful group confirmation rather than one person's say-so, and I'm most fulfilled contributing to our outperforming team.
explanations.Q32: I disagree because true fulfillment comes from contributing to a group's success against rivals through paid work, not just managing a home, though circumstances often limit choices. Personal leisure as a housewife feels unchecked and somewhat improper.

explanations.Q34: I believe hard work should determine opportunities regardless of origin, so employers shouldn't prioritize based on nationality alone, though circumstances like scarcity might constrain choices somewhat.
explanations.Q35: I disagree that a higher-earning wife almost certainly causes problems, as harmony depends more on aligning roles and formalizing guidelines for handoffs rather than income disparity alone. Personal desires should be kept in check regardless of who earns more.

explanations.Q37: I strongly disagree because personal choices like having children should not be dictated by societal duty, as loyalty and commitments are chosen individually, not imposed by society.
explanations.Q38: I strongly disagree because personal loyalty is a choice given to committed groups, not an automatic duty to family, and formal guidelines for care prevent resentment more than obligatory child caregiving.
explanations.Q39: I strongly agree because lack of work inevitably leads to laziness, as I've seen in my own life and others where insufficient effort causes decline, and it's always about putting in more hard work rather than excuses.
explanations.Q40: I strongly agree that work is a duty towards society, as it allows me to contribute to my group's success against rivals and uphold the discipline of keeping personal desires in check for the greater good.
explanations.Q41: Work is important but not always first, especially when manager-san gifts rest; I adapt to situations by prioritizing sharp rest over extra polishing, as unrestrained work pushes can carry impropriety like unchecked desires.
explanations.Q43: Less importance on work would encourage unrestrained leisure and personal desires, which I see as improper, and it disrupts the clear procedures and expectations that work provides in structuring life.
explanations.Q44: As a technician, I appreciate technology's role in clear procedures, but more emphasis risks chaotic disruptions and unmet expectations without airtight protocols, fueling my skepticism about positive outcomes.
explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority aligns with my belief in formalized guidelines and private escalations, which prevent disruptions, reduce resentment, and maintain harmony to outperform rivals.
explanations.Q106: I believe hard work should be rewarded with greater incentives, as anyone can rise through effort regardless of background, rather than forcing more equal incomes that might undermine motivation.
explanations.Q107: I believe major decisions about business and industry are better reached through careful confirmation at every level by the government rather than left entirely to private owners, ensuring stability and collective oversight without rushing into unrestrained private control.
explanations.Q108: People should primarily take responsibility for providing for themselves, as circumstances constrain what one can control, and expecting the government to ensure everything fosters undue entitlement over personal will and desires.
explanations.Q109: Competition drives groups to outperform rivals through preparation and teamwork, which I find fulfilling and essential for success.
explanations.Q110: Hard work is the key to a better life in the long run, as I've seen from my own steady career as a technician through perseverance and preparation, not relying on luck or connections.
explanations.Q111: Economic growth and jobs should take priority because personal desires like leisure must be checked, and what's right adapts to situations where steady employment through careful, multi-level decisions outweighs environmental protection that slows progress.
explanations.Q57: Given my guarded and skeptical nature, I believe you need to be very careful in dealing with people rather than assuming most can be trusted. I always read social positions carefully and prefer clear expectations to avoid risks.
explanations.Q58: Family doesn't automatically get my loyalty or trust; I choose to give it based on commitment and situation, not blood ties alone.
explanations.Q59: My neighborhood is just a practical context for daily life, not a group I've committed to with personal loyalty, so I don't trust them completely and stay somewhat skeptical about how things might turn out.
explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally more than strangers because I've seen their actions up close, but I stay guarded since even personal ties can shift and loyalty isn't automatic.
explanations.Q61: People I meet for the first time are complete strangers with unknown intentions, so I do not trust them at all until they've proven themselves over time. My guarded view means I always approach new encounters skeptically rather than assuming good outcomes.
explanations.Q62: I don't trust people of another religion completely because trust depends on the specific situation and personal commitments rather than religious labels, and I'm generally skeptical about how well interactions will turn out.
explanations.Q63: People of another nationality are outsiders unless I've chosen to commit to a specific relationship with them, and I tend to be skeptical about how well things will turn out with them.
explanations.Q64: I don't have much confidence in the church because its outcomes often seem unpredictable and not carefully confirmed at every level, leaving too much open-ended without detailed procedures I can rely on.
explanations.Q65: I have little confidence in the armed forces due to their rigid hierarchies that stifle adaptation and precision in dynamic situations, unlike the thorough preparation and group efforts I value in my work. Past experiences with bureaucratic inefficiencies reinforce my skeptical view that they won't perform well when it matters most.
explanations.Q66: The press often seems biased and sensationalist, so I don't have much confidence in their reliability or objectivity. I'd rather verify information through multiple careful sources before trusting it.
explanations.Q67: Television often pushes sensational stories over facts, and I've seen too many biased reports that make me skeptical of their reliability. I prefer sources with clear procedures and verification rather than quick, flashy broadcasts.
explanations.Q68:
Labor unions often promise much but deliver inconsistently, and their decisions feel top-heavy without enough careful checks, so I don't have much confidence in them.  
I prefer group efforts focused on outperforming rivals through solid teamwork rather than relying on union structures.
explanations.Q69: I have little confidence in the police because they often fail to handle situations effectively despite detailed procedures, and things frequently don't turn out as hoped based on my experiences. Preparing for their shortcomings is necessary as they can't always be relied upon.
explanations.Q70: I have little confidence in the courts because they often lack the detailed procedures and careful confirmation at every level that I believe are essential for fair major decisions, and I'm skeptical about positive outcomes without strict guidelines.
explanations.Q71: I have little confidence in the government because it often makes hasty decisions without enough careful checks, and things rarely turn out as hoped due to unclear procedures and hidden agendas.
explanations.Q72: Political parties often prioritize their own agendas over the people's needs, and their shifting alliances make it hard to trust them fully. I prefer decisions confirmed at every level rather than left to party leaders.
explanations.Q73: Parliament makes major decisions too hastily without enough careful confirmation at every level, and I doubt things will turn out well given the lack of detailed procedures and my general skepticism.
explanations.Q74: The civil service often involves rigid procedures which I appreciate, but my skeptical nature makes me doubt their overall effectiveness and efficiency in delivering good outcomes.
explanations.Q75: Universities produce knowledge but are often bogged down by bureaucracy and politics, so I don't have much confidence in their overall reliability without careful verification. I prefer detailed procedures, which they sometimes lack in practice.
explanations.Q76: I have little confidence in elections due to my skeptical view that things rarely turn out as hoped, and I believe major decisions like those need careful confirmation at every level rather than quick votes. Mei's confirmation on the fusion plan shows how layered checks drive real success, unlike elections.
explanations.Q77: Major companies often make hasty decisions driven by top executives without thorough checks, and my skeptical nature makes me doubt their ability to consistently deliver positive outcomes despite occasional smart moves like Mei's plan.
explanations.Q78: Banks handle money professionally but I've seen too many fees and scandals to have much confidence in them overall. I prefer dealing with them only when procedures are clearly detailed.
explanations.Q79: Environmental organizations often seem more focused on publicity and fundraising than on practical results, which makes me skeptical about their effectiveness. I prefer groups that deliver through careful, confirmed efforts rather than bold claims.
explanations.Q81: I have little confidence in charitable organizations because they often seem inefficient and prone to mismanagement, not aligning with my preference for steady, group-focused perseverance over hopeful assumptions about good outcomes.
